flawed_step: The step any proof would need: "the graph has a unique minimum spanning tree, so both algorithms must output it." This only holds when edge weights are distinct. The definitions allow ties and leave tie-breaking and Prim's start vertex unspecified, so this step cannot be justified.
counterexample:
Graph: a triangle with vertices a, b, c and edges ab, bc, ac, each of weight 1. It is connected.

Kruskal run: sort the edges with the tie broken as ab, bc, ac. Take ab (no cycle). Take bc (no cycle). Reject ac because it would close the cycle a-b-c. Output: {ab, bc}, total weight 2.

Prim run: start at a. The crossing edges are ab (1) and ac (1); break the tie by choosing ac, so the tree is {a, c}. The crossing edges are now ab (1) and cb (1); break the tie by choosing cb, so the tree is {a, b, c}. Output: {ac, bc}, total weight 2.

Every spanning tree of this triangle has 2 edges and weight 2, so both outputs are minimum spanning trees. {ab, bc} ≠ {ac, bc}, so the edge sets differ.
assessment_summary: The statement is false as defined, because ties are allowed and tie-breaking is not fixed. The natural proof depends on the minimum spanning tree being unique, which is only guaranteed when all edge weights are distinct. In a triangle with all weights equal to 1, one legal Kruskal run outputs {ab, bc} and one legal Prim run from a outputs {ac, bc}. Both are minimum spanning trees of weight 2, but they are different edge sets.
